question: An operations team runs one large workload through Claude: several thousand short, repetitive record summaries, plus one difficult reconciliation that decides how the whole set is interpreted. Everything currently runs on the deepest-reasoning tier and the allowance is gone by Wednesday. What should the team do first?
options: A) Ask for a larger allowance before making any change, since the current work is valuable and the shortfall is only a couple of days.
B) Cut the length of every prompt in the workload, so that each individual request costs less and the allowance stretches further.
C) Move the whole workload to the fastest and cheapest tier, then see over the next few weeks whether anyone complains about quality.
D) Separate the bulk repetitive work from the one genuinely difficult piece, so each part can be matched to what it actually needs.
correct_answers: D) Separate the bulk repetitive work from the one genuinely difficult piece, so each part can be matched to what it actually needs.
explanations: Asking for more allowance funds the existing pattern rather than examining it, and it leaves thousands of routine summaries consuming the most expensive capacity available for no additional benefit.

Shorter prompts trim the cost of each request but leave the real problem untouched: routine work is still being run on the tier reserved for difficult reasoning, so the same imbalance recurs next week.

Moving everything down applies one answer to two very different tasks, and the reconciliation is exactly the piece that would suffer. Waiting for complaints is a poor detection mechanism for degraded reasoning.

Correct. The workload is not one thing. Splitting the high-volume routine part from the small part that genuinely needs deep reasoning is what makes any sensible tier decision possible, and it is where nearly all the waste is.
